claim: The gill skeleton of cartilaginous fishes exhibits a striking anterior–posterior polarity, with branchial rays projecting from the posterior margin of the gill arch cartilages.
source: The gill skeleton of cartilaginous fishes (sharks, skates, rays, and holocephalans) exhibits a striking anterior–posterior polarity, with a series of fine appendages called branchial rays projecting from the posterior margin of the gill arch cartilages.
evidence: This is a descriptive anatomical observation supported by the skeletal preparations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Branchial rays derive from a posterior domain of pharyngeal arch mesenchyme that is responsive to Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling from a distal gill arch epithelial ridge (GAER) signaling centre in skate.
source: We previously demonstrated in the skate (Leucoraja erinacea) that branchial rays derive from a posterior domain of pharyngeal arch mesenchyme that is responsive to Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling from a distal gill arch epithelial ridge (GAER) signaling centre.
evidence: This claim references previous work by the authors and is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Genes encoding several Wnt ligands are expressed in the ectoderm immediately adjacent to the skate GAER.
source: Here, we show that genes encoding several Wnt ligands are expressed in the ectoderm immediately adjacent to the skate GAER, and that these Wnt signals are transduced largely in the anterior arch environment.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Wnt signals from the GAER-adjacent ectoderm are transduced largely in the anterior arch environment.
source: Here, we show that genes encoding several Wnt ligands are expressed in the ectoderm immediately adjacent to the skate GAER, and that these Wnt signals are transduced largely in the anterior arch environment.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis of Wnt target genes shown in Figure 4.

claim: Inhibition of Wnt signalling results in an anterior expansion of Shh signal transduction in developing skate gill arches.
source: Using pharmacological manipulation, we show that inhibition of Wnt signalling results in an anterior expansion of Shh signal transduction in developing skate gill arches, and in the formation of ectopic anterior branchial ray cartilages.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IWR1 treatment experiments and Ptc2 expression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Inhibition of Wnt signalling results in the formation of ectopic anterior branchial ray cartilages.
source: Using pharmacological manipulation, we show that inhibition of Wnt signalling results in an anterior expansion of Shh signal transduction in developing skate gill arches, and in the formation of ectopic anterior branchial ray cartilages.
evidence: This is demonstrated by skeletal preparations of IWR1-treated embryos shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Ectodermal Wnt signalling contributes to gill arch skeletal polarity in skate by restricting Shh signal transduction and chondrogenesis to the posterior arch environment.
source: Our findings demonstrate that ectodermal Wnt signalling contributes to gill arch skeletal polarity in skate by restricting Shh signal transduction and chondrogenesis to the posterior arch environment and highlights the importance of signalling interactions at embryonic tissue boundaries for cell fate determination in vertebrate pharyngeal arches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing Wnt inhibition leads to anterior expansion of Shh signaling and ectopic cartilage formation.

claim: Pharyngeal arches form as iterative outpockets of foregut endoderm contact the overlying surface ectoderm.
source: Pharyngeal arches form as iterative outpockets of foregut endoderm contact the overlying surface ectoderm, and this meeting of endoderm and ectoderm generates columns lined laterally by ectoderm, medially by endoderm, and containing a core of mesoderm and neural crest-derived mesenchyme (Graham and Smith, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pharyngeal arch development, supported by citation.

claim: In fishes, endodermal outpockets fuse with the overlying surface ectoderm, giving rise to the gill slits and the respiratory surfaces of the gills.
source: In fishes, endodermal outpockets fuse with the overlying surface ectoderm, giving rise to the gill slits and the respiratory surfaces of the gills (Gillis and Tidswell, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In amniotes, endodermal outpockets give rise to glandular tissues, such as the tonsils, parathyroid, and ultimobranchial glands.
source: In amniotes, endodermal outpockets give rise to glandular tissues, such as the tonsils, parathyroid, and ultimobranchial glands (Grevellec and Tucker, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The largely neural crest-derived mesenchyme of the pharyngeal arches gives rise to the pharyngeal skeleton.
source: The largely neural crest-derived mesenchyme of the pharyngeal arches gives rise to the pharyngeal skeleton – i.e., the skeleton of the jaws and gills in fishes, and of the jaw, auditory ossicles, and larynx in amniotes (Jiang et al., 2002; Kague et al., 2012; Sleight and Gillis, 2020; Couly and Le Douarin, 1990)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mesenchymal derivatives of each pharyngeal arch receive patterning and polarity information via signals from adjacent epithelia.
source: with mesenchymal derivatives of each arch receiving patterning and polarity information via signals from adjacent epithelia (Veitch et al., 1999; Gillis et al., 2009a, Couly et al., 2002; Brito et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: All jawed vertebrates belong to one of two lineages: cartilaginous fishes or bony vertebrates.
source: All jawed vertebrates belong to one of two lineages: cartilaginous fishes (sharks, skates, rays, and holocephalans) or bony vertebrates (ray- and lobe-fined fishes, with the latter including tetrapods).
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: The gill arch skeleton of both cartilaginous and bony fishes ancestrally consisted proximally of two principal gill arch cartilages (the epi- and ceratobranchials).
source: While the gill arch skeleton of both cartilaginous and bony fishes ancestrally consisted proximally of two principal gill arch cartilages (the epi- and ceratobranchials), the gill arch skeleton of cartilaginous fishes additionally includes a distal series of fine cartilaginous rods called branchial rays (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical statement supported by skeletal preparations shown in Figure 1.

claim: The gill arch skeleton of cartilaginous fishes additionally includes a distal series of fine cartilaginous rods called branchial rays.
source: While the gill arch skeleton of both cartilaginous and bony fishes ancestrally consisted proximally of two principal gill arch cartilages (the epi- and ceratobranchials), the gill arch skeleton of cartilaginous fishes additionally includes a distal series of fine cartilaginous rods called branchial rays (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by skeletal preparations in Figure 1.

claim: Branchial rays originate along the posterior margin of the epi- and ceratobranchial cartilage, and curve posteriorly as they project into the interbranchial septum of each arch.
source: These rays reflect the clear anteroposterior polarity of the gill arch skeleton of cartilaginous fishes, originating along the posterior margin of the epi- and ceratobranchial cartilage, and curving posteriorly as they project into the interbranchial septum of each arch (Gillis et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is an anatomical observation supported by citation and visible in Figure 1.

claim: Elasmobranch cartilaginous fishes possess five sets of branchial rays, associated with their hyoid and first four gill arches.
source: Elasmobranch cartilaginous fishes (sharks, skates, and rays) possess five sets of branchial rays, associated with their hyoid and first four gill arches.
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation based on established knowledge.

claim: Holocephalans possess a single set of branchial rays supporting their hyoid arch-derived operculum.
source: Holocephalans, on the other hand, possess a single set of branchial rays supporting their hyoid arch-derived operculum (Gillis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The branchial rays of cartilaginous fishes develop under the influence of the GAER, a Sonic hedgehog (Shh)-expressing signaling centre located within the posterior–distal epithelium of the gill arches.
source: The branchial rays of cartilaginous fishes develop under the influence of the GAER (gill arch epithelial ridge): a Sonic hedgehog (Shh)-expressing signaling centre located within the posterior–distal epithelium of the gill arches (Gillis et al., 2009b; Gillis and Hall, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Shh signaling from the GAER is asymmetrically transduced within the posterior arch environment, as evidenced by posterior expression of Ptc2.
source: As the gill arches undergo a prolonged phase of lateral expansion, Shh signaling from the GAER is asymmetrically transduced within the posterior arch environment, as evidenced by posterior expression of Ptc2 (Gillis and Hall, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Ptc2 is a Shh co-receptor and transcriptional readout of Shh signaling.
source: as evidenced by posterior expression of Ptc2 (Gillis and Hall, 2016) – a Shh co-receptor and transcriptional readout of Shh signaling (Pearse et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ptc2 function, supported by citation.

claim: In skate, branchial rays derive exclusively from posterior–distal (Shh-responsive/GAER-adjacent) gill arch mesenchyme.
source: in skate, branchial rays derive exclusively from posterior–distal (Shh-responsive/GAER-adjacent) gill arch mesenchyme, application of exogenous Shh protein within gill arches is sufficient to induce ectopic branchial ray formation, and targeted or systemic inhibition of hedgehog signaling using cyclopamine results in branchial ray deletion (Gillis et al., 2009b; Gillis and Hall, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Application of exogenous Shh protein within gill arches is sufficient to induce ectopic branchial ray formation.
source: in skate, branchial rays derive exclusively from posterior–distal (Shh-responsive/GAER-adjacent) gill arch mesenchyme, application of exogenous Shh protein within gill arches is sufficient to induce ectopic branchial ray formation, and targeted or systemic inhibition of hedgehog signaling using cyclopamine results in branchial ray deletion (Gillis et al., 2009b; Gillis and Hall, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Targeted or systemic inhibition of hedgehog signaling using cyclopamine results in branchial ray deletion.
source: in skate, branchial rays derive exclusively from posterior–distal (Shh-responsive/GAER-adjacent) gill arch mesenchyme, application of exogenous Shh protein within gill arches is sufficient to induce ectopic branchial ray formation, and targeted or systemic inhibition of hedgehog signaling using cyclopamine results in branchial ray deletion (Gillis et al., 2009b; Gillis and Hall, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Shh is expressed in the GAER of the hyoid and first four gill arches of skate embryos.
source: In developing skate gill arches, Shh is expressed in the GAER (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The GAER region includes the Shh-expressing GAER, as well as adjacent Shh-responsive (i.e. Ptc2+) tissues.
source: (D) The dissected GAER region includes the Shh-expressing GAER, as well as adjacent Shh-responsive (i.e. Ptc2+) tissues, as indicated by multiplexed mRNA in situ hybridization by chain reaction (HCR) for Shh and Ptc2 on paraffin section.
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiplexed HCR shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 401 genes were upregulated in the GAER region compared to non-GAER tissues.
source: We used a false discovery rate of 5% and no log fold-change (LogFC) cut-off to generate a list of 401 genes that were upregulated in the GAER region.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Functional enrichment analysis indicated enrichment of Wnt signaling pathway components in the GAER region.
source: Differentially expressed genes were subjected to functional enrichment analysis, and this analysis indicated enrichment of Wnt signaling pathway components in the GAER region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for enrichment analysis).
evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in the GAER region included those encoding the Wnt ligands Wnt2b, Wnt3, Wnt4, Wnt7b, and Wnt9b.
source: Differentially expressed genes in the GAER region included those encoding the Wnt ligands Wnt2b, Wnt3, Wnt4, Wnt7b, and Wnt9b, the transmembrane Wnt inhibitors Kremen1 (Mao et al., 2002) and APCDD1 (Shimomura et al., 2010), and the secreted Wnt antagonist Notum (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in the GAER region included those encoding the transmembrane Wnt inhibitors Kremen1 and APCDD1.
source: Differentially expressed genes in the GAER region included those encoding the Wnt ligands Wnt2b, Wnt3, Wnt4, Wnt7b, and Wnt9b, the transmembrane Wnt inhibitors Kremen1 (Mao et al., 2002) and APCDD1 (Shimomura et al., 2010), and the secreted Wnt antagonist Notum (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis, with citations supporting the functional roles of these genes.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in the GAER region included the secreted Wnt antagonist Notum.
source: Differentially expressed genes in the GAER region included those encoding the Wnt ligands Wnt2b, Wnt3, Wnt4, Wnt7b, and Wnt9b, the transmembrane Wnt inhibitors Kremen1 (Mao et al., 2002) and APCDD1 (Shimomura et al., 2010), and the secreted Wnt antagonist Notum (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis, with citation supporting the functional role of Notum.

claim: Wnt7b is co-expressed with Shh in the cells of the GAER.
source: We found that while Wnt7b was co-expressed with Shh in the cells of the GAER (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiplexed HCR shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Wnt2b, Wnt3, Wnt4, and Wnt9b are all expressed predominantly in the epithelium immediately adjacent to the GAER.
source: Wnt2b, Wnt3, Wnt4, and Wnt9b (Figure 3B–E) were all expressed predominantly in the epithelium immediately adjacent to the GAER.
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiplexed HCR shown in Figures 3B-E.

claim: Apcdd1 is expressed in the GAER and anterior–distal mesenchyme.
source: We found that Apcdd1 was expressed in the GAER and anterior–distal mesenchyme (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Notum is expressed in the anterior–distal mesenchyme.
source: Notum in the anterior–distal mesenchyme (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Kremen1 is expressed in the anterior (GAER-adjacent) epithelium.
source: and Kremen1 in the anterior (GAER-adjacent) epithelium (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Broad transcription of Axin2 throughout distal gill arch tissues indicates that Wnt signaling within this territory is occurring through the canonical/β-catenin pathway.
source: Finally, broad transcription of Axin2 throughout distal gill arch tissues (Figure 4D) indicates that Wnt signaling within this territory is occurring through the canonical/β-catenin pathway (Lustig et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on Axin2 expression data shown in Figure 4D and citation supporting Axin2 as a canonical Wnt pathway marker.

claim: Some Wnt signals emanating from the GAER or GAER-adjacent epithelium are transduced preferentially within the anterior arch environment, in a pattern that is largely complimentary to the posterior epithelial and mesenchymal transduction of Shh signals from the GAER.
source: our spatial expression data nevertheless indicate that some Wnt signals emanating from the GAER or GAER-adjacent epithelium are transduced preferentially within the anterior arch environment, in a pattern that is largely complimentary to the posterior epithelial and mesenchymal transduction of Shh signals from the GAER.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial expression patterns of Wnt ligands and target genes shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The GAER is of endodermal origin.
source: In 8/29 embryos, we recovered CM-DiI labeling up to and including the Shh-expressing cells of the GAER in one or more pharyngeal arches (Figure 5C–C''), indicating the endodermal origin of these cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by CM-DiI lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Wnt-expressing epithelium immediately anterior to the GAER derives from the ectoderm.
source: Together, these observations indicate that the GAER is of endodermal origin and arises at the ectoderm–endoderm interface during pharyngeal arch development and that the Wnt-expressing epithelium immediately anterior to the GAER derives from the ectoderm.
evidence: This is inferred from the CM-DiI lineage tracing experiments showing no labeling of epithelium anterior to the GAER.

claim: The GAER arises at the ectoderm–endoderm interface during pharyngeal arch development.
source: Together, these observations indicate that the GAER is of endodermal origin and arises at the ectoderm–endoderm interface during pharyngeal arch development and that the Wnt-expressing epithelium immediately anterior to the GAER derives from the ectoderm.
evidence: This is inferred from the lineage tracing data showing endodermal origin of GAER and ectodermal origin of adjacent anterior epithelium.

claim: IWR1-treated embryos showed a marked reduction in the expression of Axin2 throughout their gill arches.
source: IWR1-treated embryos showed a marked reduction in the expression of Axin2 throughout their gill arches (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR on IWR1-treated embryos shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: IWR1 treatment resulted in a reduction in the expression of Apcdd1 in the GAER and anterior–distal gill arch mesenchyme.
source: as well as a reduction in the expression of Apcdd1 in the GAER and anterior–distal gill arch mesenchyme (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR on IWR1-treated embryos shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: IWR1 treatment resulted in a complete loss of Notum expression in anterior–distal gill arch mesenchyme.
source: and a complete loss of Notum expression in anterior–distal gill arch mesenchyme (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR on IWR1-treated embryos shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: IWR1 treatment effectively suppressed canonical Wnt signaling from the GAER and GAER-adjacent epithelium.
source: These findings indicate that our drug treatment effectively suppressed canonical Wnt signaling from the GAER and GAER-adjacent epithelium, including those signals transduced asymmetrically in the anterior gill arch environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in expression of Wnt target genes (Axin2, Apcdd1, Notum) following IWR1 treatment.

claim: Shh is a pro-chondrogenic signal from the GAER in skate gill arches.
source: Shh is a pro-chondrogenic signal from the GAER in skate gill arches (Gillis et al., 2009b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IWR1 treatment resulted in no noticeable change in the expression of Shh in the GAER.
source: While we observed no noticeable change in the expression of Shh or in the spatial distribution of Ptc2 transcripts in gill arch mesenchyme with IWR1 treatment, we did note a qualitative increase in Ptc2 expression within the normal mesenchymal domain and a clear anterior expansion of Ptc2 expression within the epithelium adjacent to the GAER (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR on IWR1-treated embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: IWR1 treatment resulted in no change in the spatial distribution of Ptc2 transcripts in gill arch mesenchyme.
source: While we observed no noticeable change in the expression of Shh or in the spatial distribution of Ptc2 transcripts in gill arch mesenchyme with IWR1 treatment, we did note a qualitative increase in Ptc2 expression within the normal mesenchymal domain and a clear anterior expansion of Ptc2 expression within the epithelium adjacent to the GAER (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR on IWR1-treated embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: IWR1 treatment resulted in a qualitative increase in Ptc2 expression within the normal mesenchymal domain.
source: While we observed no noticeable change in the expression of Shh or in the spatial distribution of Ptc2 transcripts in gill arch mesenchyme with IWR1 treatment, we did note a qualitative increase in Ptc2 expression within the normal mesenchymal domain and a clear anterior expansion of Ptc2 expression within the epithelium adjacent to the GAER (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR on IWR1-treated embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: IWR1 treatment resulted in a clear anterior expansion of Ptc2 expression within the epithelium adjacent to the GAER.
source: While we observed no noticeable change in the expression of Shh or in the spatial distribution of Ptc2 transcripts in gill arch mesenchyme with IWR1 treatment, we did note a qualitative increase in Ptc2 expression within the normal mesenchymal domain and a clear anterior expansion of Ptc2 expression within the epithelium adjacent to the GAER (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR on IWR1-treated embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: GAER-adjacent Wnt signaling restricts the transduction of pro-chondrogenic Shh signaling in the anterior gill arch territory in skate.
source: This points to a role for GAER-adjacent Wnt signaling in restricting the transduction of pro-chondrogenic Shh signaling in the anterior gill arch territory in skate.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Wnt inhibition leads to anterior expansion of Shh signal transduction.

claim: IWR1-treated embryos had several distinct phenotypic changes, including smaller size, a loss of gill filaments and disrupted fin morphology.
source: IWR1-treated embryos had several distinct phenotypic changes, including smaller size, a loss of gill filaments and disrupted fin morphology (the latter consistent with previous findings of Nakamura et al., 2015; Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by whole embryo images in Figure 7 and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Branchial rays articulate exclusively with the posterior margin of the gill arch cartilages in skate.
source: The skate hyoid and gill arch skeleton include branchial rays that articulate exclusively with the posterior margin of the gill arch cartilages (Gillis et al., 2009a – see also Figure 1).
evidence: This is an anatomical observation supported by citation and visible in Figure 1.

claim: Branchial rays invariably develop on the posterior side of the interbranchial muscle plate.
source: These rays also invariably develop on the posterior side of the interbranchial muscle plate – a histologically and molecularly distinct derivative of the paraxial mesodermal core that extends down the middle of each pharyngeal arch (Daniel, 1934; Graham, 2008; Hirschberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an anatomical observation supported by citations.

claim: Skate embryos reared in DMSO control seawater showed no gill arch skeletal defects (n=4 embryos).
source: Skate embryos reared in DMSO control seawater showed no gill arch skeletal defects (n=4 embryos; Figure 7Ai)
evidence: This is demonstrated by skeletal preparations shown in Figure 7Ai.

claim: Embryos reared in IWR1 seawater possessed conspicuous ectopic branchial rays in the anterior gill arch territory (n=7/8 embryos).
source: while embryos reared in IWR1 seawater possessed conspicuous ectopic branchial rays in the anterior gill arch territory (n=7/8 embryos; Figure 7Bi).
evidence: This is demonstrated by skeletal preparations shown in Figure 7Bi.

claim: Ectopic branchial rays occurred along the entire dorsoventral axis of the arch and ranged from short cartilage rods located in the anterior–distal gill arch to nearly full-length branchial rays.
source: These ectopic branchial rays occurred along the entire dorsoventral axis of the arch and ranged from short cartilage rods located in the anterior–distal gill arch to nearly full-length branchial rays that extended much of the way toward the gill arch cartilages.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation of the ectopic cartilages visible in Figure 7.

claim: In control embryos, branchial rays always developed on the posterior side of the mesodermally-derived interbranchial muscle plate of each gill arch.
source: In section, branchial rays of skate embryos reared in DMSO control seawater always developed, as per normal, on the posterior side of the mesodermally-derived interbranchial muscle plate of each gill arch: this was evident from histochemical staining and from HCR for the chondrocyte markers Sox9 and Col2a1 (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological sections and HCR shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: In IWR1-treated embryos, ectopic branchial rays were consistently located anterior to the interbranchial muscle plate.
source: Conversely, in skate embryos reared in IWR1 seawater, ectopic branchial rays were consistently located anterior to the interbranchial muscle plate (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological sections and HCR shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: The induction of ectopic branchial rays with IWR1 treatment suggests that Wnt signaling contributes to the maintenance of anteroposterior polarity of the skate gill arch skeleton by repressing chondrogenesis in the anterior gill arch.
source: The induction of ectopic branchial rays with IWR1 treatment suggests that Wnt signaling contributes to the maintenance of anteroposterior polarity of the skate gill arch skeleton by repressing chondrogenesis in the anterior gill arch and may do so by restricting transduction of GAER Shh signaling to the posterior gill arch territory.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing ectopic cartilage formation upon Wnt inhibition.

claim: Wnt signaling may contribute to gill arch skeletal polarity by restricting transduction of GAER Shh signaling to the posterior gill arch territory.
source: The induction of ectopic branchial rays with IWR1 treatment suggests that Wnt signaling contributes to the maintenance of anteroposterior polarity of the skate gill arch skeleton by repressing chondrogenesis in the anterior gill arch and may do so by restricting transduction of GAER Shh signaling to the posterior gill arch territory.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the combined observations of Wnt inhibition leading to both anterior expansion of Shh signaling and ectopic cartilage formation.

claim: Wnt–Shh signaling antagonism at the pharyngeal ectodermal–endodermal tissue boundary is a key molecular regulator of cell fate determination and anatomical polarity within the developing gill arch skeleton of the skate.
source: These findings suggest that Wnt–Shh signaling antagonism at the pharyngeal ectodermal–endodermal tissue boundary is a key molecular regulator of cell fate determination and anatomical polarity with the developing gill arch skeleton of the skate (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the combined experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: WNT2B and WNT9B are expressed in the pharyngeal arch ectoderm of the chick.
source: Previous analyses have reported the expression of several Wnt genes in developing craniofacial tissues of bony vertebrates (Summerhurst et al., 2008), including the expression of WNT2B and WNT9B in the pharyngeal arch ectoderm of the chick (Geetha-Loganathan et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Wnt9b is expressed in the first and second pharyngeal arches in zebrafish.
source: Wnt9b in the first and second pharyngeal arches in zebrafish (Jezewski et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Wnt4a is expressed in zebrafish pharyngeal ectoderm.
source: Wnt4a in zebrafish pharyngeal ectoderm (Choe et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Wnt9a and Wnt5b are expressed in zebrafish oral epithelium.
source: and Wnt9a and Wnt5b in zebrafish oral epithelium (Dougherty et al., 2013; Rochard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: β-catenin-independent (i.e. non-canonical) Wnt signaling plays a crucial role in epithelial remodeling during the early formation of pharyngeal endodermal pouches in zebrafish.
source: While β-catenin-independent (i.e. non-canonical) Wnt signaling plays a crucial role in epithelial remodeling during the early formation of pharyngeal endodermal pouches in zebrafish (Choe et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Non-canonical Wnt signaling plays a role in maturation and morphogenesis of the zebrafish oropharyngeal skeleton.
source: and in maturation and morphogenesis of the zebrafish oropharyngeal skeleton (Rochard et al., 2016; Ling et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling has been implicated in patterning of the pharyngeal arch-derived skeleton in multiple taxa.
source: canonical Wnt signaling has been implicated in patterning of the pharyngeal arch-derived skeleton in multiple taxa.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the specific examples that follow in the text.

claim: Blocking canonical Wnt signaling causes disrupted facial cartilage formation, including reductions of Meckel's and ceratohyal cartilages in zebrafish.
source: Blocking canonical Wnt signaling causes disrupted facial cartilage formation, including reductions of Meckel's and ceratohyal cartilages in zebrafish (Alexander et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of ectodermal canonical Wnt signaling in mouse causes loss of facial bones with hypoplasia of all facial prominences.
source: and loss of ectodermal canonical Wnt signaling in mouse causes loss of facial bones with hypoplasia of all facial prominences (Reid et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In mouse and human, cleft palate phenotypes may arise as a consequence of mutations in Wnt3 and Wnt9b.
source: Furthermore, in mouse and human, cleft palate phenotypes may arise as a consequence of mutations in Wnt3 and Wnt9b (Niemann et al., 2004; Juriloff et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Perturbation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling has been implicated in CATSHL syndrome, a human developmental disorder involving craniofacial bone malformation and mispatterning of the pharyngeal arches.
source: and perturbation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling has been implicated in CATSHL syndrome, a human developmental disorder involving craniofacial bone malformation and mispatterning of the pharyngeal arches (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The role for canonical Wnt signaling in patterning the gill arch skeleton of skate may reflect broadly conserved roles for this pathway in pharyngeal skeletal development across jawed vertebrates.
source: Our finding of a role for canonical Wnt signaling in patterning the gill arch skeleton of skate may, therefore, reflect broadly conserved roles for this pathway in pharyngeal skeletal development across jawed vertebrates, though with the skate's possession of branchial rays offering a unique anatomical readout of anterior–posterior polarity defects that arise within the pharyngeal arch-derived skeleton in response to perturbations.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on comparison with other vertebrates.

claim: In chick, misexpression of WNT5A/5B promotes early chondrogenesis of limb bud mesenchyme in vitro and delays the terminal differentiation of growth plate chondrocytes in vivo.
source: In some instances, Wnt signaling functions to promote skeletogenesis: for example, in chick, misexpression of WNT5A/5B promotes early chondrogenesis of limb bud mesenchyme in vitro and delays the terminal differentiation of growth plate chondrocytes in vivo (Church et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In mouse, canonical WNT signaling from cranial ectoderm induces specification of osteoblast progenitors of cranial dermal bone within underlying mesenchyme.
source: and in mouse, canonical WNT signaling from cranial ectoderm induces specification of osteoblast progenitors of cranial dermal bone within underlying mesenchyme (Goodnough et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In chick, signaling through WNT3, 4, 7A, 14 or FZ7 have all been shown to inhibit chondrogenesis in vitro or in vivo.
source: In chick, signaling through WNT3, 4, 7 A, 14 or FZ7 have all been shown to inhibit chondrogenesis in vitro or in vivo (Rudnicki and Brown, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In mouse, conditionally induced haploinsufficiency of the gene encoding the β-catenin degradation complex component APC results in loss of resting zone chondrocytes and their clonal progeny in developing growth plates.
source: while in mouse conditionally induced haploinsufficiency of the gene encoding the β-catenin degradation complex component APC (i.e. activation of canonical Wnt signaling) results in loss of resting zone chondrocytes and their clonal progeny in developing growth plates (Hallett et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Genes encoding WNT ligands are expressed in the limb bud ectoderm.
source: In the limb bud, genes encoding WNT ligands are expressed in the ectoderm (Kengaku et al., 1998; Parr et al., 1993; Geetha-Loganathan et al., 2005; Summerhurst et al., 2008)

claim: WNT ligands in the limb bud ectoderm function synergistically with fibroblast growth factor signaling from the apical ectodermal ridge to inhibit chondrogenesis of limb bud mesenchyme and to promote soft connective tissue fates.
